diagnostic_evidence.quote: Then, the solution $\X(t)$ at a given time satisfies the following $N$-dimensional Sylvester equation:
we can solve for $y_{i_1i_2\ldots i_N}$ in \eqref{e:TjYC}, if and only if

issues.failure_explanation: The abstract and Section 3 present the procedure as computing X(t) for any system with constant coefficients. The theorem only says X(t) satisfies a Sylvester equation. That equation is solved by dividing by sum_j t_{j,i_j i_j}, which is possible only when every sum of one eigenvalue per A_j is nonzero. The ODE solution exists for all t even when this fails, for example for a pair of rotation generators with eigenvalues +i and -i, or for Neumann-type diffusion matrices that have a zero eigenvalue. In those cases the Sylvester equation does not determine X(t), and the algorithm divides by zero. The nonsingularity hypothesis is never stated for the ODE application.

failure_location.quote: the method allows to compute the solution of linear $N$-dimensional systems of ODEs of constant coefficients at any time $t$

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: State the nonvanishing-eigenvalue-sum hypothesis explicitly in the abstract, in Section 3 and in the implementation of the theorem, and restrict the claim to that case.
issues.overall_effect: The scope claim for ODEs and evolutionary PDEs is overstated. The ODE solver (Theorem 3.1 plus the Schur-based algorithm) is valid only under an unstated spectral condition. The theorem itself, as a necessary condition, remains true.
issues.title: ODE application claimed for any constant-coefficient system, but the method needs a nonsingular Kronecker sum
issues.why_classification: A limited weakening of the advertised scope fixes it and leaves a comparable result. Treating the singular case would need new work, so it is more than a minor wording fix.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: has a unique solution $\X\in\CC^{n_1\times n_2}$, if and only if
In what regards the uniqueness of the solution, the coefficients are uniquely determined from \eqref{e:yi1i2iN} in a recursive way.

issues.failure_explanation: Nonzero eigenvalue sums are equivalent to unique solvability for every right-hand side, not to existence of a solution. If some sum vanishes, the linear operator is singular. The equation still has solutions (infinitely many) for right-hand sides in its range, for example B = 0. So 'have a solution iff' is false as stated. The introduction gives the correct 'unique solution' form for N = 2, and the recursion only determines Y when all denominators are nonzero.

failure_location.quote: have a solution if and only if, when taking an eigenvalue of each matrix $\A_j$, their sum is always different from zero

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the claim with: for every right-hand side the equation has a unique solution iff all sums of one eigenvalue from each A_j are nonzero. If a sum vanishes, it is singular.
issues.overall_effect: The solvability statement for the N-dimensional Sylvester equation is misstated. The algorithm itself is unaffected.
issues.title: Existence of a solution wrongly characterized as equivalent to nonzero eigenvalue sums
issues.why_classification: A one-sentence wording correction preserves the method and all results.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: calculate accurately the computational cost required

issues.failure_explanation: The paper counts one division per entry y_{i_1...i_N}, so the total is P = n_1...n_N divisions, not P*N. Even with the paper's own P*N, the displayed terms sum as follows. Write S = sum_j n_j. Then (P/2)(5S-N) + (P/2)(5S-3N-2) + PN = P(5S-N-1), not P(5S-N+1). With the correct P divisions the total is P(5S-2N). The stated exact flop count is therefore wrong in two places.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Use P divisions and recompute the total as P(5S-2N), or consistently keep P*N divisions and write P(5S-N-1).
issues.overall_effect: The 'accurate' exact cost formula is incorrect in its lower-order terms. The leading term 5PS and the asymptotic estimate 5N n^(N+1) are unaffected.
issues.title: Operation count for Y and the final flop total are arithmetically inconsistent
issues.why_classification: Local recomputation fixes it, and the leading-order complexity conclusions are unchanged.

issues.failure_explanation: For u = f(t) exp(-|x|^2) one gets Delta u + 2 x.grad u + (2N+1)u = f exp(-|x|^2). The PDE then reduces to f' = f - 1, with general solution f = 1 + C e^t. The stated solution has C = 1, so f(0) = 2. The initial condition u(x,0) = exp(-x.x) requires f(0) = 1, which gives C = 0 and u = exp(-x.x). Thus (1+e^t)exp(-x.x) does not solve the stated initial-value problem, and the reported error against it is not a valid accuracy measurement for the problem as posed.

failure_location.quote: Moreover, the solution of \eqref{e:uxt} is $u(\xx, t) = (1+\exp(t))\exp(-\xx\cdot\xx)$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Change the initial condition to 2 exp(-x.x), consistent with the stated exact solution, and confirm that the listing uses it.
issues.overall_effect: The validation of the PDE application (the reported 1e-13 accuracy) is inconsistent with the problem as stated.
issues.title: Stated exact solution of the advection-diffusion test violates the stated initial condition
issues.why_classification: A local correction of the problem data restores a valid test, and the method and conclusions are untouched.

issues.failure_explanation: The displayed formula with the extra factor 2^(-n) gives monic polynomials: H_1 = x and H_2 = x^2 - 1/2. The normalization constant 1/(pi^(1/4) sqrt(2^n n!)) in psi_n is correct only for H_n(x) = (-1)^n e^(x^2) d^n/dx^n e^(-x^2), which gives 2x and 4x^2-2. With the paper's H_1 = x, the L^2 norm of psi_1 is 1/2 rather than 1. The two definitions are inconsistent.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Remove the factor 1/2^n so that H_n is the standard Hermite polynomial.
issues.overall_effect: The definition of the Hermite polynomials and functions is wrong as written. The numerics use the external herdif routine and are unaffected.
issues.title: Rodrigues formula given for H_n does not match the Hermite function normalization
issues.why_classification: A one-factor correction suffices, and no result depends on it.
